snip.t: Immune system (specifically T-lymphocytes): CD4+ T-lymphocytes are central to cell-mediated immunity, particularly against intracellular pathogens and fungi like *Pneumocystis jirovecii*.
The inflammatory component is driven by Th2-type T lymphocytes which facilitate IgE synthesis through production of IL-4 and eosinophilic inflammation through IL-5
● NHL is a diverse group of solid tumors which occurs with the malignant transformation and growth\nof B or T lymphocytes or their precursors in the lymphatic system.
T-lymphocyte defects (congenital or acquired by chemotherapy, AIDS, or malignancy) are associated with an increased risk of Listeria monocytogenes infections of the CNS.
Immune system: Macrophages (phagocytosis, granuloma formation), T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity, cytokine production), granuloma structure (caseous necrosis, fibrous cuff).
The risk of PCP significantly increases as the CD4+ T-lymphocyte count drops.
The CD4+ T-lymphocyte: The central coordinator of adaptive cell-mediated immunity.

qs.q: An immunology student examines a secondary lymphoid organ. Where are naive T lymphocytes predominantly localized within a lymph node before encountering their specific antigen?
o: Primary B cell follicles of cortex
Paracortical zone rich in dendritic cells
qs.e: Naive T cells populate the paracortex of lymph nodes, where they scan professional antigen-presenting cells.

qs.q: A 4-year-old boy with a history of recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections is evaluated. Serum protein electrophoresis shows markedly reduced gamma globulin levels, while absolute T-lymphocyte counts are normal. What is the underlying developmental defect?
o: Defective class switching of surface immunoglobulins on lymphocytes
Defective thymic epithelial development leading to absent T cells
Mutated phagocytic enzyme systems failing to produce superoxide ions
Absent complement component C3 impairing classical pathway activation
Failure of pre-B cells to mature into functional circulating B cells
qs.e: X-linked agammaglobulinemia involves a defect in Bruton tyrosine kinase, preventing the maturation of pre-B cells into mature B cells.

qs.q: In the context of tumor immunity, cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) kill tumor cells. Which molecule on the CTL mediates the killing?
o: Engagement of antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity pathways
Binding of Fas ligand expressed on the cytotoxic cell
Release of perforin and granzymes from cytotoxic granules
Initiation of complement-mediated lysis of target cells
Triggering of macrophage phagocytosis of the tumor cells
qs.e: CTLs kill target cells by releasing perforin and granzymes, which induce apoptosis in the target cell.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Cellular Immunology Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which clinical feature is characteristic of T-lymphocyte defects, whether congenital or acquired via chemotherapy, AIDS, or malignancy?
o: High incidence of Streptococcus pneumoniae empyema
Increased risk of Listeria monocytogenes CNS infections
Predilection for Gram-negative enteric shunt abscesses
qs.e: T-lymphocyte defects are associated with an increased risk of Listeria monocytogenes infections of the CNS. Neisseria infections are instead linked to complement and properdin pathway deficiencies.

qs.q: A 19-year-old university student presents with fever, severe pharyngitis, generalized lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. A peripheral blood smear reveals atypical lymphocytes. What is the primary host cell type destroyed by cytotoxic T-lymphocytes in this condition?
o: Dendritic cells located in lymph nodes
Epithelial cells located in salivary glands
qs.e: Infectious mononucleosis caused by EBV induces a host response where cytotoxic T-lymphocytes appear as atypical lymphocytes to destroy EBV-infected B-cells. Epithelial cells serve as the initial site of viral replication rather than the target of CTL destruction.
qs.s: Herpesviruses: HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Tx: MCQs

qs.q: A 25-year-old man presents with a well-circumscribed, pigmented skin lesion on his trunk that has developed a symmetric, surrounding zone of depigmentation over the past two months. Histologic examination of the depigmented margin reveals a dense dermal infiltrate composed predominantly of CD8+ T lymphocytes surrounding nevus cells. What is the underlying pathophysiologic process of this finding?
o: Complement-mediated microvascular thrombosis in the dermis
Host immune response directed against melanocytes
Malignant clonal proliferation of atypical keratinocytes
Granulomatous destruction of dermal elastic fibers
qs.e: A halo nevus involves a T-cell-mediated immune response targeting shared antigens on both nevus cells and normal epidermal melanocytes. Granulomatous destruction of elastic fibers is characteristic of other dermal elastolytic conditions rather than immune-mediated depigmentation.
qs.s: Pigmentation & Melanocyte Disorders: Nevi, Freckles Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: A virology student analyzes a chronic viral infection where the host liver damage is primarily driven by cytotoxic T lymphocytes attacking infected hepatocytes rather than direct viral cytopathic effects. Which virus typically exhibits this pathogenesis?
qs.e: Hepatitis B liver damage is largely immune-mediated, caused by the host's own cytotoxic T lymphocytes and inflammation rather than direct viral killing. Rhinovirus and rotavirus cause acute lytic infections rather than immune-mediated chronic hepatitis.
qs.s: Medical Virology Semester 3 Crash Revision: MCQs

qs.q: Which subtype of T lymphocytes directly targets and destroys infected or cancerous cells presenting foreign antigens?
qs.e: Cytotoxic T cells directly target and destroy infected, cancerous, or foreign antigen-presenting cells. Helper T cells assist other cells by releasing cytokines rather than directly killing targets.

ai.title: T Lymphocytes and Clinical Immunology
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: T cells drive cell‑mediated immunity, coordinate cytokine responses and determine susceptibility to intracellular infections. Understanding their subsets, lab assessment and common deficits guides bedside decisions in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: T lymphocytes are mature thymic‑derived white blood cells that recognise antigen presented on MHC molecules. CD4+ helper T cells orchestrate immune responses; CD8+ cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells. Their balance is crucial for defence against viruses, intracellular bacteria, fungi and for vaccine efficacy.
b: Develop in thymus, undergo positive and negative selection
Express T‑cell receptor (TCR) with CD3 complex
Require IL‑2 for proliferation after activation

sections.p: T cells lack surface immunoglobulin; instead they display a clonally unique TCR. Subsets are defined by surface markers (CD4, CD8) and cytokine profiles (Th1, Th2, Th17, Treg).
b: Th1 → IFN‑γ, activates macrophages (important for TB, leishmaniasis)
Th2 → IL‑4, IL‑5, IL‑13, drives IgE and eosinophilia (asthma, helminths)
Th17 → IL‑17, recruits neutrophils (fungal infections)
Treg → IL‑10, TGF‑β, maintains tolerance

sections.p: Clinically relevant T‑cell defects are either primary (genetic) or secondary (acquired). In low‑resource East African hospitals the most common secondary deficits are HIV infection, malnutrition, and chemotherapy for cancers.
b: HIV → progressive CD4+ loss, opportunistic infections (PCP, TB, cryptococcal meningitis)
Severe malnutrition → reduced thymic output, low CD4+ counts
Chemotherapy/rituximab → lymphopenia, increased bacterial/fungal sepsis

sections.p: Assess quantity and function of T cells. In settings without flow cytometry, surrogate clinical clues guide management.

t.b: How many functional helper T cells are present? → <200 cells/µL predicts high risk of PCP; 200‑350 cells/µL indicates need for prophylaxis against opportunists.
What is the balance of cytotoxic to helper T cells? → Low ratio (<1) suggests advanced HIV; high ratio may indicate immune reconstitution.
Is cell‑mediated immunity intact? → Anergy (no induration) points to severe T‑cell dysfunction.

sections.p: Management focuses on correcting the underlying cause, preventing opportunistic infections, and supporting immune recovery.
b: Start antiretroviral therapy (ART) promptly in HIV; monitor CD4+ rise.
Nutritional rehabilitation (protein‑rich diet, micronutrients) improves thymic output.
Prophylaxis: trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole when CD4+ <200 cells/µL; fluconazole for CD4+ <100 cells/µL in endemic areas.
Avoid high‑dose steroids unless indicated, as they further suppress T cells.

sections.p: Examiners test integration of immunology with bedside reasoning.
b: Link low CD4+ count to specific opportunistic infections.
Explain why PCP prophylaxis is started at <200 cells/µL.
Distinguish Th1‑driven diseases (TB, leishmaniasis) from Th2‑driven (helminths, allergic asthma).

whenToSeekHelp: Severe opportunistic infection (e.g., cryptococcal meningitis, disseminated TB) in a patient with known low CD4+ count
Rapid CD4+ decline >50 cells/µL in a month despite ART
Unexplained persistent fever with neutropenia and lymphopenia

faq.q: Why does PCP become common when CD4+ falls below 200 cells/µL?
faq.a: CD4+ cells are essential for recruiting macrophages and producing cytokines that control Pneumocystis; their loss impairs clearance.

faq.q: Can a normal CD4+ count rule out HIV‑related immune dysfunction?
faq.a: No; functional defects can exist early, and CD8+ expansion or high viral load may still indicate risk.

faq.q: What bedside sign suggests severe T‑cell deficiency?
faq.a: Recurrent oral thrush or chronic diarrhoea with weight loss in a young adult is a red flag.

exam: A 32‑year‑old HIV patient presents with dry cough and fever; CD4+ count is 180 cells/µL. What is the next immediate step? — Start empiric PCP prophylaxis (TMP‑SMX) and obtain sputum for Pneumocystis staining.

A malnourished child has persistent oral thrush despite antifungal therapy. Which immune parameter should you assess and why? — Measure CD4+ count; low values explain susceptibility and guide nutritional/ART interventions.

In a patient on chemotherapy for lymphoma, you note a CD4+ count of 150 cells/µL but no infections yet. What prophylactic measures are indicated? — Begin TMP‑SMX for PCP and consider fluconazole if local cryptococcal prevalence is high.

How does a Th1‑dominant response protect against intracellular bacteria, and which cytokine is pivotal? — IFN‑γ activates macrophages to kill intracellular organisms such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

A patient with severe asthma shows high eosinophil count and elevated IgE. Which T‑cell subset is driving this and what cytokine would you target? — Th2 cells; IL‑5 is key for eosinophil survival, targeted by anti‑IL‑5 agents.

Why is high-dose corticosteroid therapy contraindicated in a patient with active TB and low CD4+ count? — Steroids further suppress Th1 responses, worsening bacterial control and increasing mortality.

Explain why a CD4/CD8 ratio <1 is more prognostic than absolute CD4+ count in early HIV infection. — The ratio reflects immune dysregulation; a falling ratio predicts faster progression even when CD4+ numbers are still modest.

A refugee from a schistosomiasis‑endemic area presents with eosinophilia and cough. Which T‑cell subset is likely predominant and what does this imply for treatment? — Th2 predominance; treat with praziquantel and consider anti‑IL‑4/IL‑5 strategies if severe eosinophilic lung disease.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused history and a systematic physical exam reveal clues to T‑cell quantity, function and the pattern of opportunistic disease in low‑resource settings.
b: Duration of symptoms and any recent opportunistic infection (e.g., cough, fever, skin lesions, oral thrush).
Known HIV status, CD4+ count (if known), ART adherence, recent viral load, or other immunosuppressive conditions (malnutrition, chemotherapy, steroids).
Weight loss, growth failure in children, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, or unusual skin lesions suggesting Th1, Th2 or Th17 deficiency.
Vaccination history (BCG, measles, varicella) and prior prophylaxis (TMP‑SMX, fluconazole).
Exposure history: TB contacts, endemic helminths, fungal spores, or recent travel to high‑risk areas.

t.b: Look for wasting, lymphadenopathy, oral thrush, or skin rashes; suggests chronic T‑cell depletion or specific subset dysfunction.

t.a: Palpation of lymph nodes (cervical, axillary, inguinal)
t.b: Enlarged, firm nodes may indicate chronic infection (TB) or lymphoma; soft, tender nodes suggest acute viral infection.
Scraping reveals white plaques that can be wiped (candida) versus ulcerative lesions (HSV, CMV); candida points to CD4+ <200 cells/µL.
Crackles or wheeze may indicate TB (Th1) or asthma/helminth‑related eosinophilia (Th2); auscultation cannot differentiate pathogen.

t.a: Skin examination for papules, nodules, or depigmented patches
t.b: Hypopigmented halo around a melanoma suggests CTL‑mediated immune attack; cannot confirm specific T‑cell subset.
Signs of cryptococcal meningitis (headache, papilledema) hint at CD4+ <50 cells/µL; bedside exam cannot measure CD4+ directly.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Laboratory and point‑of‑care tests answer whether T‑cell numbers are low, whether function is impaired, and which opportunistic infection is present.
b: Full blood count with differential – lymphopenia (<1 000 cells/µL) supports T‑cell loss; neutrophilia may point to bacterial superinfection.

CD4+ T‑cell count (flow cytometry) – <200 cells/µL triggers PCP prophylaxis; <50 cells/µL triggers cryptococcal antigen screening; <100 cells/µL (or <50 in endemic areas) triggers fluconazole prophylaxis.
CD4/CD8 ratio – ratio <1.0 in chronic HIV suggests advanced disease; normal ratio does not exclude early depletion.
Serum cryptococcal antigen – positive at any CD4+ level warrants pre‑emptive fluconazole; negative does not rule out early infection.
GeneXpert MTB/RIF on sputum – detects TB in Th1‑dominant disease; a positive result guides anti‑TB therapy regardless of CD4+ count.
Serum IgE and eosinophil count – elevated values suggest Th2‑driven helminth infection or allergic asthma; does not measure T‑cell function.
IL‑2 receptor (sCD25) – elevated in active immune activation (e.g., severe HIV); not routinely available, use clinical surrogates if absent.

t.b: Answers quantitative T‑cell status; >500 cells/µL is normal, 200‑499 moderate, <200 severe, <50 very severe. If flow cytometer unavailable, use clinical scoring (weight, opportunistic infections).
Helps calculate CD4/CD8 ratio; high CD8+ with low CD4+ may indicate chronic viral infection. Not diagnostic alone.
Screen for invasive fungal disease (e.g., PCP) when CD4+ <200; positive supports PCP but needs confirmatory microscopy.
Identifies interstitial infiltrates typical of PCP, cavitary lesions of TB, or lymphadenopathy; cannot specify pathogen.
Detects acid‑fast bacilli; positive confirms TB in Th1‑dominant disease.
Shows CD8+ infiltrate in melanoma regression; confirms CTL activity but not systemic T‑cell count.

sections.p: Combine clinical, laboratory and imaging data to stage T‑cell immunodeficiency and prioritize management.
b: Diagnose T‑cell deficiency when CD4+ <200 cells/µL or when recurrent opportunistic infections occur despite normal absolute lymphocyte count.
Stage HIV‑related T‑cell loss: Stage 1 CD4+ ≥500, Stage 2 350‑499, Stage 3 200‑349, Stage 4 <200 cells/µL (AIDS‑defining).
Severity of opportunistic infection: PCP mild (outpatient), moderate (hospitalised, O₂ < 94 %), severe (respiratory failure).
TB severity: pulmonary vs disseminated; use WHO clinical classification (Category I vs II) plus CD4+ count for adjunctive steroids.
Malnutrition grading (WHO): moderate (weight‑for‑age Z‑score –2 to –3) may lower CD4+ by ~20 %; severe (<‑3) may require urgent nutritional rehabilitation before ART.

sections.p: Several diseases mimic T‑cell deficiency or present with similar opportunistic patterns; careful differentiation avoids mismanagement.

t.b: Presents with low CD4+ from birth, facial anomalies, thymic hypoplasia; differentiate by congenital features and absence of HIV risk factors.
Normal CD4+ count, recurrent bacterial infections, absent serum Ig; differentiate by normal T‑cell function tests and low immunoglobulins.
Causes functional T‑cell suppression with normal CD4+ count; look for medication history and reversible lymphopenia after taper.
Low CD4+ but no HIV antibodies; differentiate by negative rapid HIV test and presence of kwashiorkor/ marasmus signs.
Transient lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes; CD4+ may be normal; differentiate by heterophile antibody test and self‑limited course.

sections.p: Begin with rapid assessment, confirm T‑cell deficiency, then initiate definitive therapy, monitor response, and decide when to refer to specialist care.
b: 1. Immediate history of infections, vaccination, travel, drug use and family history of immunodeficiency.
2. Physical exam: lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, skin lesions, oral thrush, respiratory signs.
3. Confirm diagnosis: CD4+ count, CD4/CD8 ratio, flow cytometry if available; otherwise use clinical surrogates (e.g., persistent thrush).
4. Start definitive treatment: antiretroviral therapy for HIV; nutritional rehabilitation for malnutrition; immunoglobulin if hypogammaglobulinemia; consider prophylaxis per CD4 thresholds.
5. Initiate prophylaxis: trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole for CD4+ <200; fluconazole for CD4+ <50; consider azithromycin for MAC if CD4+ <50.
6. Monitor: repeat CD4+ every 3–6 months, clinical review for new infections, drug side‑effects, adherence.
7. Escalate: if CD4+ <200 and no improvement, refer to infectious disease or transplant centre; if severe cytopenia or organ failure, consider hematology referral.
8. Avoid high‑dose steroids unless life‑threatening; avoid live vaccines; avoid nephrotoxic drugs in renal impairment.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse effects, interactions and management strategies for common drugs used in T‑cell deficiency.
b: 1. Trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole: rash, Stevens‑Johnson, hyperkalemia, nephrotoxicity; monitor renal function, electrolytes, CBC; avoid in severe renal failure.
2. Fluconazole: hepatotoxicity, drug interactions with CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers; monitor LFTs, avoid in severe hepatic disease.
3. Antiretroviral therapy: lipodystrophy, neuropathy, hepatotoxicity, myopathy; monitor LFTs, CBC, lipid profile; avoid nephrotoxic ART in renal failure.
4. Immunoglobulin: anaphylaxis, aseptic meningitis, volume overload; pre‑test for IgA deficiency, monitor vitals during infusion.
5. Corticosteroids: immunosuppression, hyperglycaemia, hypertension; use lowest effective dose, taper slowly, monitor glucose and BP.
6. Herbal remedies: St. John’s wort, ginseng may reduce ART levels; counsel patients to avoid or disclose use.

sections.p: Recognise early signs of serious complications and know when to refer or intensify therapy.
b: 1. Persistent fever >48h despite antibiotics: suspect opportunistic infection; refer for imaging and microbiology.
2. New neurological deficits: consider cryptococcal meningitis or CNS lymphoma; urgent lumbar puncture and referral.
3. Severe cytopenia (ANC <500, platelets <50k): consider marrow failure; refer to haematology.
4. Uncontrolled hyperglycaemia or hypertension in steroid therapy: adjust dose, refer to endocrinology.
5. Hepatic dysfunction with rising transaminases on fluconazole or ART: stop drug, refer to hepatology.
6. Recurrent infections despite prophylaxis: evaluate adherence, drug levels, consider alternative prophylaxis.

sections.p: Factors that alter presentation, investigations or treatment in T‑cell deficiency.
b: 1. HIV: accelerates CD4 decline, alters drug metabolism, increases risk of TB and fungal infections.
2. TB: may mask or mimic opportunistic infections; requires concurrent ATT and careful drug interaction monitoring.
3. Malnutrition: reduces thymic output, blunts vaccine response, increases drug toxicity; provide protein‑rich diet and micronutrients.
4. Pregnancy: altered immune state, some ART teratogenic, avoid live vaccines, monitor fetal growth.
5. Diabetes: increases infection risk, complicates steroid use, monitor glucose closely.
6. Herbal remedies: can induce CYP enzymes, reducing ART efficacy; counsel patients.
7. Alcohol: hepatotoxic, interferes with ART metabolism, increases risk of pancreatitis.
8. Renal or hepatic failure: dose adjustments for ART, TMP‑SMX, fluconazole; avoid nephrotoxic drugs.
9. Age extremes: infants have immature immunity, elderly have comorbidities; tailor monitoring and drug choice.

sections.p: Tailored management for key populations with T‑cell deficiency.
b: 1. Children: use weight‑based dosing, monitor growth, consider early vaccination schedules, avoid live vaccines if CD4+ <200.
2. Pregnancy: prefer efavirenz‑based ART after first trimester, avoid fluconazole >200 mg/day, monitor fetal growth, counsel on breastfeeding.
3. Elderly: higher risk of drug toxicity, monitor renal/hepatic function, adjust ART doses, consider drug–drug interactions with polypharmacy.
4. People with HIV: integrate ART with prophylaxis, monitor viral load, counsel on adherence, screen for TB and hepatitis.
5. Low‑resource settings: use point‑of‑care CD4 testing, rely on clinical surrogates, prioritize TMP‑SMX and fluconazole, use generic ART, involve community health workers.

facts: CD4+ count <200 cells/µL: start PCP prophylaxis with TMP‑SMX
Normal CD4/CD8 ratio in healthy adults is 1.5–2.5; inversion (<1.0) is typical in chronic HIV
Th1 cells produce IFN‑γ, essential for macrophage activation against TB and leishmaniasis
Th2 cells produce IL‑4, IL‑5, IL‑13, driving IgE and eosinophilia in asthma and helminths
Th17 cells secrete IL‑17, recruiting neutrophils for fungal infections
Treg cells produce IL‑10 and TGF‑β, maintaining self‑tolerance
IL‑2 is required for T‑cell proliferation after antigen recognition

vivas.q: Why is high‑dose corticosteroid therapy contraindicated in a patient with active TB and a low CD4+ count?
vivas.a: Steroids further suppress cell‑mediated immunity, increasing risk of disseminated TB and opportunistic infections

vivas.q: A malnourished child has persistent oral thrush despite antifungal therapy. Which immune parameter is most likely deficient?
vivas.a: Low CD4+ T‑cell count due to impaired thymic output from malnutrition

vivas.q: Explain how a Th1‑dominant response protects against intracellular bacteria and name the pivotal cytokine.
vivas.a: IFN‑γ activates macrophages to kill ingested bacteria; IFN‑γ is the key cytokine

vivas.q: A patient with severe asthma shows high eosinophil count and elevated IgE. Which T‑cell subset is driving this response?
vivas.a: Th2 cells, producing IL‑4, IL‑5, IL‑13

vivas.q: A 4‑year‑old boy has recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections, low gamma globulin, normal T‑cell counts. What defect is most likely?
In tumor immunity, which molecule on a cytotoxic T lymphocyte mediates target cell killing?
vivas.a: Perforin and granzymes released via the immunological synapse

vivas.q: Which clinical feature is characteristic of T‑lymphocyte defects, whether congenital or acquired?
vivas.a: Recurrent viral infections, especially herpesviruses, and poor vaccine responses

vivas.q: A 19‑year‑old presents with fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes. What is the primary host cell type destroyed?
vivas.a: CD4+ T lymphocytes are the main target of Epstein‑Barr virus

vivas.q: A 25‑year‑old with a pigmented skin lesion shows a surrounding zone of depigmentation. Histology shows loss of melanocytes. What is the likely diagnosis?
vivas.a: Tinea versicolor (Malassezia), but the depigmentation suggests pityriasis versicolor; however, the question likely refers to vitiligo secondary to autoimmune T‑cell attack

vivas.q: A chronic viral infection causes liver damage primarily by cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Which virus is most likely?
vivas.a: Hepatitis B virus, where CTLs mediate hepatocyte destruction

vivas.q: Which subtype of T lymphocytes directly targets and destroys infected or cancerous cells presenting foreign antigens?
Which type of immunity is primarily mediated by T lymphocytes targeting intracellular pathogens and tumor cells?
What bedside sign would you look for to assess for ascites in a patient with suspected liver disease?
vivas.a: Shifting dullness: percussion over the abdomen shows dullness that shifts with position, indicating fluid

vivas.q: If a patient has a CD4+ count of 150 cells/µL but no infections, what is the likely explanation?
vivas.a: Recent ART initiation leading to CD4+ rise, or transient lymphopenia due to stress or infection

vivas.q: Why is fluconazole prophylaxis recommended only when CD4+ <50 cells/µL?
vivas.a: Risk of cryptococcal meningitis rises sharply below 50 cells/µL; prophylaxis reduces incidence

mcqs.q: A 28‑year‑old HIV patient with CD4+ 180 cells/µL presents with cough. Which prophylaxis is indicated?
A patient with a CD4+ count of 45 cells/µL is at risk for which opportunistic infection?
mcqs.e: Cryptococcal meningitis risk rises below 50 cells/µL

mcqs.q: Which cytokine is produced by Th1 cells to activate macrophages?
A 35‑year‑old with severe asthma has high IgE. Which T‑cell subset is responsible?
mcqs.e: Th2 cells drive IgE and eosinophilia

mcqs.q: Which drug is NOT used for PCP prophylaxis?
mcqs.e: Bacitracin is not an antibiotic for PCP

mcqs.q: A patient with a CD4/CD8 ratio <1.0 in early HIV infection indicates?

mistakes: Confusing CD4+ count thresholds for PCP and cryptococcal prophylaxis
Assuming CD4/CD8 inversion is universal in early HIV
Overlooking the need for fluconazole prophylaxis when CD4+ <50 cells/µL
Misidentifying Th2 cytokines as Th1 cytokines
Using steroids in active TB without considering immunosuppression
Failing to recognize that atypical lymphocytes indicate EBV infection
Misattributing low gamma globulin to T‑cell defect instead of B‑cell defect
Assuming all opportunistic infections occur only when CD4+ <200 cells/µL
